1:
Gill marks the courage of the return: these were cities of Lycaonia, and in the second of them Paul had been stoned, yet he goes there again, none of these things moving him from the preaching of the gospel. Barnes observes that Luke drops Barnabas at this point and confines the narrative to Paul, and holds it impossible to determine which of the two towns Timothy belonged to, where Robertson and Ellicott make him a native of Lystra. Henry treats the passage as an adoption, Paul a spiritual father taking a disciple of Christ to be his own disciple, and notes that one design of the book is to help us understand the epistles, two of which are addressed to this man. Ellicott reads it as the first mention of a name afterwards so dear to the Apostle.

On his age they agree within a year or two. Barnes argues from the later charge that no man despise his youth, Ellicott sets him at not more than eighteen or twenty, Robertson at about eighteen, and Clarke says he must have been very young, since years afterwards there was still danger that his youth would prejudice his ministry. Henry names the mother Eunice and the grandmother Lois and commends both for their unfeigned faith. Whether the father was a proselyte is disputed. Ellicott thinks it probable, since the child had been trained in the sacred books from infancy, and thinks it probable too that the father was still living; Clarke makes him either a mere heathen or at most a proselyte of the gate who never submitted to circumcision; and Robertson and Barnes argue backwards from the son, that a proselyte would have had Timothy circumcised.

Why the son was uncircumcised is answered from the law. Henry says the entail of the covenant and its seal went, as other entails did in that nation, by the father and not by the mother, so that Timothy was neither obliged to circumcision nor entitled to it unless when grown he should himself desire it; and though his mother could not prevail to have him circumcised in infancy she educated him in the fear of God, that though he wanted the sign of the covenant he might not want the thing signified. On the marriage itself Henry holds the prohibition ran equally both ways, though it seems limited to the nations living among them in Canaan, from whom infection was most feared, while Barnes thinks the law was simply not much regarded by Jews living in the midst of heathen nations.

The good report is where Calvin and Robertson do their work. Calvin says Luke states it plainly so that we may know Paul did nothing rashly or without good consideration, and that Paul here observes in his own case the choice he elsewhere commands in choosing ministers. He then raises an apparent disagreement, that Luke has the testimony come from the brethren while Paul requires a bishop to be well reported of by those without, and answers that we must principally look to the judgment of the godly, who alone are meet witnesses and alone discern rightly according to the Spirit of God, attributing no more to the wicked than to blind men; yet in the second place even infidels should be brought to commend him, lest the Church be exposed to their slanders and evil speaking. Robertson finds in the imperfect a continuous witness borne in both towns, and draws the rule that the approval of the local church is a wise precaution before the licensing and ordaining of a preacher. Clarke notes that one editor would repunctuate the sentence so that the report attaches to Timothy and not his father, which Gill and Barnes assert without it. Ellicott adds that a good report from Iconium as well as Lystra shows Timothy already employed in carrying on intercourse between the two churches.
3:
Gill notes the young man had grace, considerable gifts for the ministry and a good testimony, so that Paul was desirous of him as a companion. Barnes makes the choice exemplary: Paul called forth talent that might be usefully employed, since Timothy would never have thought of it himself, and valued proper qualifications, a good reputation, talents and prudence, and a careful training in the Scriptures.

Five men defend the circumcision, all measuring it against the refusal to circumcise Titus. Clarke gives the practical reason, that the Jews would neither have heard Timothy preach nor had any connection with him, and that Paul could have had no access to them had they known he associated with an uncircumcised man, both being counted unclean; the act was merely prudential, not done to seek justification by law. Robertson puts the difference in the stakes: with Titus the whole principle of Gentile liberty was at issue, whereas Timothy, being both Jew and Greek, would have given continual offence with no advantage to that cause and could not have preached in the synagogues at all; a question of efficient service, not of salvation, and cites another that Timothy was circumcised because of Jewish unbelievers, not believers. Ellicott gives three reasons: the act was spontaneous, and men may concede as a favour what they would rightly resist when demanded as a necessity; Timothy's mixed parentage made him by the received canons inherit from the nobler side and stand by birth as an Israelite, where Titus was a Greek pure and simple; and by not urging circumcision before baptism the Apostle had shown he did not hold it essential. Barnes reduces it to expediency for peace, Wesley to the unbelieving Jews, who would not have conversed with him.

Calvin alone asks whether the sign could lawfully be used once abolished. It was no sacrament as Abraham's was, but an indifferent ceremony serving for the nourishing of love, not for any exercise of godliness; and he sets out three degrees: that Christ's coming so abolished the ceremonies that they no longer belonged to God's worship, figured nothing and carried no necessity; that their use nevertheless remained free until the gospel should more plainly appear; and that they might be retained only so far as the use served edification and fostered no superstition. He then draws the line that decides the case: circumcision did not stand where the sacrifices stood, ordained for expiating sins, so Paul might lawfully circumcise Timothy and might not have offered a sacrifice for sin.

Whether the decrees were permanent divides Robertson from Calvin. Robertson takes the perfect participle for the permanence of the Jerusalem conclusions and the present infinitive for a charter of liberty for continual living, not a temporary compromise, with the imperfect a delivery kept up city by city. Calvin holds they continued only for a time, since as soon as the danger of offence ceased Paul unburdened the churches and made free what the apostles had forbidden, which cancels nothing they decreed, since they never meant a perpetual law but only to mitigate what might hurt weak consciences. On the word Clarke reports a contention that the term rendered decrees is a gloss, only the things judged standing originally, the Syriac reading the decrees that were written; Barnes takes it for the proper term for a royal edict; Ellicott argues the number of copies implied guarantees Luke's transcript faithful. On the growth, Clarke says the disputes at Antioch had spread far and unhinged many, the decrees coming in good time; Robertson reads the strengthening as making firm and solid like the muscles, and the increase as a continuous revival; and Calvin, treating the decrees as put in by the way, says the far other fruit Luke commends is that the churches were confirmed in the faith, which stays itself on the pure Word of God and not on men's laws.
6:
Why the Spirit shut two doors is the question here. Henry offers three answers and prefers the third: that Asia did not need them, other hands being at work; that the people were not yet prepared; or that Christ meant to employ Paul in new work among a Roman colony, the Gentiles he had reached hitherto being Greeks, and the Romans more particularly hated by the Jews. He finds in it an intimation that the light of the gospel would in aftertimes be directed more westward than eastward. Barnes says it flatly, that God meant to carry the gospel into Greece, this prohibition being the means of its first introduction into Europe. Clarke makes it a matter of readiness, God sending his servants where the word would be received.

Calvin refuses every account grounding the difference in the men. If these Gentiles were unworthy of salvation, we may demand why Macedonia was worthier; those who desire to be too wise assign the cause to men, that God vouchsafes his gospel as he sees a man bent to the obedience of faith, whereas he says far otherwise, that he appeared plainly to those who sought him not and spake to those who asked not of him. Whence comes aptness to be taught, or a mind to obey, but from his Spirit? To the doubt what certainty ministers can have today, certified by no oracles, he answers that Paul's charge was so wide, being to preach through Asia and Europe, that it was to sail in a most wide sea, God beckoning to him as by reaching forth his hand.

How it came is answered three ways: Henry by secret whispers in both minds, found on comparing notes to be the same and from the same Spirit, or by prophets; Barnes by direct revelation; Wesley by an inward dictate, adding that a strong impression for which we can give no account is not altogether to be despised. Henry marks the difference from an older prohibition, where the prophet was forbidden to preach at all, while these are forbidden in one place and directed to another of greater need.

The geography is disputed at two points. Clarke argues that the Asia named cannot be Asia Minor at large, since its provinces included the districts where the apostles had just preached, so only the proconsular province can be meant, which Barnes identifies with Ionia and the seven churches. Robertson works the harder question, whether Luke's phrase names one region at once Phrygian and Galatian or adds a province to a district: he sets out the northern and southern theories and rests the case on grammar, that the aorist participle rendered having been forbidden can express only simultaneous or antecedent action, never subsequent, so the topography brings Paul right up to Bithynia, which he calls the strongest argument for that view.

At the second refusal the text itself is in question. Clarke reports that many manuscripts and versions read the Spirit of Jesus rather than the Spirit, holds it undoubtedly genuine, and would restore it at once; Ellicott agrees and finds it of dogmatic importance, confirming that the Spirit stands in the same relation to the Son as to the Father; Robertson notes only that the expression occurs nowhere else. Ellicott catches the tone of the stretch, the uncertainty produced day by day by this conflict of human plans with divine direction. Robertson has them skirting Mysia and neglecting it, and reaches Troas, the seaport counted part of neither province and the place to take ship for Philippi. Gill derives Phrygia from a river or a word meaning dry; Clarke traces the names of Troy from its founders and notes that no vestige remains. Ellicott ends where the vision begins: the question that must have occupied all Paul's thoughts, where next to proclaim the glad tidings, expressed itself in prayer, and the vision answered it.
9:
Whether the vision was a dream is disputed. Barnes and Clarke say it is impossible to tell whether it came in sleep or waking, God's will having been made known at different times both ways; Gill allows either. Wesley denies the dream flatly, since no dream but two is named in the New Testament; and Calvin rests on the text, which says only that it came in the night, there being night visions men see waking. Who he was divides them too. Barnes reports the opinion that he was the province's guardian angel and finds no foundation for it; Clarke reports both that and a communication made to the imagination; Wesley takes him for an angel in the Macedonian habit representing the inhabitants; Robertson reports the modern identification with Luke, answering that whatever is true of Luke, the narrative must not be robbed of its supernatural aspect.

Robertson adds that Paul had twice been rebuffed, that most men would have gone home, that the call is now positive and not negative, and that his visions came at real crises. Ellicott says the vision explained all the promptings and drawings-back of the journey: this was the door to be opened, the faith of Christ was to pass from Asia to Europe, and the cry was a call from the whole western world. Calvin turns to the word help: since the gospel is the power of God to salvation, its ministers are said to help those who perish, and are to be received as deliverers, yet without robbing God of the best part of his praise.

Calvin will not let the vision stand alone. A bare vision leaves the mind in doubt, since Satan often abuses apparitions to cozen unbelievers, whereas truly divine ones the Spirit seals with a certain mark; and he sets beside it the wicked spirit that appeared to Brutus, inviting him to the unhappy battle fought at the very place to which Paul was afterwards called, the cause being unlike and the Lord dealing far otherwise with his servant, putting him out of doubt and not leaving him astonished. When Luke joined is settled differently by each. Clarke and Barnes suppose at Troas, the first place where the historian includes himself; Ellicott argues that since no account is given of the Evangelist's conversion he and Paul must have been acquainted already, probably at Antioch, and that the phrase the Lord had called us implies Luke was himself a preacher; Robertson argues from the plural being dropped when Paul leaves the city and resumed when he returns that Luke was in the party and no blundering copyist. Wesley remarks that Luke never names himself, and finds the like amiable modesty in all the sacred historians.

Whether Philippi may be called a chief city is the crux. Barnes reports that the province had been divided into four parts, that one version reads a city of the first part, and that some would alter the Greek, another city having been made chief of that division; he answers that in the two hundred and twenty years since, Philippi may have outgrown it, or that the phrase means the first city they reached. Clarke says it has greatly puzzled critics and gives the same defence. Ellicott grants that adverse critics cite it for Luke's inaccuracy, notes that the Greek has no article and that the epithet first is often found on coins of cities not capitals, and reads the word for part as border-land; Wesley settles it by the river that divided the province. Robertson describes the colony planted there with the full privileges of Roman citizenship. Calvin reads the sequel as a glass showing how sharply the Lord exercised their faith: they crossed the sea as though a whole nation would meet them, found none in the city to take pains with, and gained in an obscure corner one woman, an alien.
13:
Why they met by a river is answered two ways. Ellicott renders the phrase as a place where an oratory was established, and explains that where the Jews had no synagogue, as in a military station, they used river-banks, which made ablutions easy, and often obtained ground outside the walls, a practice a Roman satirist noted as an instance of the decay of the old faith. Robertson gives the same account, noting heathen writers use the word too. Calvin makes it danger rather than convenience: their religion was then most odious, and public assembly was not lawful in a Roman colony, so they withdrew into a secret corner where they could not be espied, and even that was grudged them; by their example God teaches how much account to make of the profession of faith.

Whether Lydia's name was her own or her country's Gill leaves open, since it will not settle whether she was Jewess or Gentile: she may be named from her region, a Roman poet uses it, and it may also be Jewish. Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson take it from the country, slaves and freedwomen commonly bearing such names. Both note inscriptions attesting a guild of purple-sellers there, and Robertson judges her a woman of means; Barnes adds that purple was a most valuable colour, worn chiefly by the rich.

What the opening of her heart means divides them sharply. Calvin observes that Luke assigns her aptness not to a quicker intellect nor to any preparation of her own but simply to the Lord's opening her heart; he had just commended her godliness, yet shows she could not comprehend the gospel save through the illumination of the Spirit. Clarke reads it the other way: as a sincere worshipper she was already prepared for the truths spoken, and being faithful to the grace received she was given more, so that it is wrong to suppose she had no light of God before. Wesley stands between: the Greek properly refers to opening the eyes, the heart has its eyes, closed by nature, and to open them is the peculiar work of God. Chrysostom praises the calling: a woman, of low condition, and from her trade too, yet of elevated mind, God's calling her bearing testimony to her.

Her household baptism is the disputed point. Barnes calls it a strong presumptive proof of household baptism, since her believing is mentioned while theirs is not, and it is manifestly implied they were baptized because she believed; Wesley asks who can believe that in so many families there was no infant, or that Jews long used to circumcise their children would not now devote them to God by baptism. Ellicott answers that this is to read a great deal between the lines, that the utmost that can be said is that the language does not exclude infants, and that the practice rests on firmer grounds than a precarious induction from ambiguous passages, no evidence appearing that she had children or a husband. Robertson quotes the objection that the Greek may mean her servants or work-people, and adds that in the household baptisms one sees infants or not according to his predilections. Calvin says nothing of infants and draws a rule instead: Lydia consecrated her family to God, and the faithful should so order their houses that each may be an image of the Church.

On her constraining them Chrysostom marks her wisdom: nothing could be more persuasive than if ye have judged me faithful, leaving the apostles to decide and yet exceedingly forcing them. Clarke gives them another sense, that her reception of the gospel proves her fidelity to the light already imparted. Wesley notes they did not comply at once, lest any think they sought their own profit; Gill supposes the baptism took place in the river beside which they met; Calvin, that from that small graft sprang a noble Church.
16:
Whether the phrase means the act or the place of prayer is settled three ways. Gill calls the first a mere Anglicism, unknown to the eastern writers, and insists on the prayer-house, since the damsel followed them for many days and knew by their going there what they were. Clarke reports that several manuscripts add the article, which makes the place emphatic and confirms the same sense. Ellicott concedes the Greek has no article, so far favouring the received rendering, but answers that the word for church is likewise used without one, as we say going to church.

What the spirit was they explain from the same fable. Henry calls her a pythoness, actuated by an evil spirit which dictated ambiguous answers that gratified the vain desire of knowing things to come and often deceived, and observes that the devil could not have gained such adoration had he not pretended to give men oracles. Barnes and Clarke tell of the serpent slain by Apollo, from which the god and his prophetesses took their name, Clarke adding that all who could predict, or pretended to, were said to be influenced by that spirit; Ellicott makes the serpent the symbol of wisdom at Delphi. Robertson observes that a later writer applied the term to ventriloquists, that the Greek Old Testament uses it of those with familiar spirits, that the word for soothsaying is akin to the verb meaning to be mad, and that Luke does not credit Apollo with a real existence. Calvin says the same in his own way, that Luke follows common speech and so exhibits the error of the common people.

Why she cried after them is harder. Barnes offers three conjectures and prefers the last: she hoped for a reward, feared expulsion and hoped to conciliate them, or saw evident tokens that their doctrine would prevail and hoped by proclaiming it to gain authority and a reputation for inspiration. Clarke finds a deep design in it: the testimony was every syllable true and yet calculated to ruin them, since the Jewish law abhorred all dealings with familiar spirits, so the Jews would conclude the apostles were in compact with demons and their miracles wrought by magic. Ellicott will not read it merely as a demon mocking: the cry shows a divided consciousness and spoke of a mind longing for deliverance, the girl seeing in the preachers those able to deliver her, as unlike as possible to the masters who traded on her maddened misery. Wesley says only that it was a great truth Paul neither needed nor would accept; Robertson, that pagan inscriptions use the same title for the Supreme Being.

Why Paul bore it so long comes last. Gill says she was suffered to continue so the expulsion might be the more manifest. Calvin supposes Paul at first neglected the crying, hoping it would vanish, but that the repetition wearied him, since long dissembling would have made Satan more insolent; and adds that Paul could not have commanded rashly, the word being vain without the commandment of God, lest any condemn him of hastiness. Barnes lists five grounds of the grief, among them her state of bondage and the system behind it that held a large part of the pagan world. Clarke observes that Paul turned to the spirit and not the woman, she being only its organ, and argues that every circumstance proves a real possession, since Luke's training as a physician equipped him to detect imposture and he finds none, speaking of spirit and damsel as distinct persons. Robertson makes the same distinction, that Paul, like his Master, distinguished the demon from the individual, and notes the cure was instantaneous. Ellicott asks whether it was not right for Paul to do as his Master had done and restore her to her true self, and refuses to think she was left to drift back into unbelief.
19:
What enraged the masters is agreed and pressed hard. Barnes observes that instead of regarding the act as proof of divine power they were intent only on their profits, and finds in their indignation an illustration of the fixedness with which men regard wealth, any interposition destroying their hopes of gain filling them with wrath. Ellicott finds a prophetic significance in the use here of the very word which was the key to nearly all the early persecutions: men could tolerate varieties of worship or the speculations of philosophers, but were roused to madness by whatever threatened their business. Robertson quotes another that the most sensitive part of civilised man is the pocket. Calvin sees the same devil in both scenes: he who had lately flattered Paul by the mouth of the maid now drives her masters into fury, changing his coat to play a tragedy where flattery could not speed. Clarke adds that the girl continued a heathen, since we hear no word of her conversion, and makes that silence an argument that the possession had been real.

The accusation is dissected by all. Calvin calls it craftily composed: on one side they pretend the name of the Romans, than which nothing was more favourable, on the other they purchase hatred by naming the Jews, whose name was then infamous, a Roman being free to sacrifice in any country where there were idols. Robertson marks the contrast between being Jews in one verse and being Romans in the next, and calls the pose of patriotism all sound and fury, since love of money moves these masters. Barnes calls it cunning and artful, since they cared nothing for the religion of Rome or of the Jews, and notes how conscientious they all at once became about the laws. Ellicott recalls that the decree banishing the Jews from Rome would be known at Philippi and give the charge special force; Wesley, that the Jews were a nation peculiarly despised by the Romans.

On the appeal to custom Calvin turns the passage against his own opponents: they lean upon a prejudice lest the cause come to be disputed, as it is said in his day that a thing was decreed in a General Council, or is too ancient to be questioned, or has long been approved by usage; all of which serve only to rob the Word of God of authority, boasting of men's decrees while leaving no place for God's laws. Wesley puts it the other way: the world has received the doctrines of all the philosophers that ever were, but gospel truth has something peculiarly intolerable to the world. Clarke supplies the ground from the Roman side, that they were very jealous of their national worship, quoting a poet and his commentator.

Who the magistrates were is settled by their titles. Gill notes the word properly signifies military captains; Clarke makes them commanders of the army, holding sovereign authority in a colony; Ellicott says the word is used with Luke's usual accuracy of the colony's praetors; Robertson observes that as they represented consuls they were attended by lictors bearing rods. Why Paul did not then claim his citizenship Ellicott raises and answers: some suppose the mob's violence made the claim impossible to hear, others question its truthfulness, but more naturally he would not assert a right securing exemption for himself alone. Wesley says either they did not immediately say it, or in the tumult it was not regarded. On the punishment Barnes and Clarke note that Rome set no limit where the Jews allowed but forty stripes save one, so the apostles had the fullest measure; Clarke describes the stocks as pierced with holes at different distances, so the legs might be forced far apart and extreme pain produced; and Ellicott and Robertson describe the inner prison, a dungeon with no light or air save through the door.
25:
Chrysostom asks what could equal these souls. Scourged, misused, in peril of their lives, thrust into the inner prison and set fast in the stocks, they did not suffer themselves to sleep but kept vigil all the night; whereas we, in our soft beds, with none to be afraid of, pass the whole night in sleep. These were the very things that made them wakeful. Barnes takes the plainer view, that their painful posture and the scourging prevented sleep, but that though they had no repose they had a quiet conscience, and that a Christian may find more true joy in a prison than a monarch on his throne. Clarke says they were so satisfied they were right and had done their duty that there was no room for regret, and prayed first for grace and for the pardon of their persecutors, then sang so heartily that the prisoners heard them from the inner prison. Gill adds that they prayed for the jailer who had used them so ill.

What they sang is a question of grammar. Ellicott and Robertson agree that the Greek expresses one act rather than two, praying they were singing; Ellicott adds that the act was habitual and would not be intermitted even when they were fastened so that they could not kneel, and that the hymn may have been a prayer-psalm, or one of those a Roman governor later described, in which men offered adoration to Christ as God. Robertson supposes portions of the Psalms with original outbursts of praise. Wesley says they sang notwithstanding weariness, hunger, stripes and blood; Henry, that the persecutors meant to dishearten them and found them heartened instead.

Whether the earthquake was miraculous divides them. Gill denies flatly that it arose from natural causes, from wind pent up in the earth, and makes it rise from the prayers of the saints going up to heaven. Barnes calls the loosing of every one's bands evidently a miracle. Ellicott says Luke apparently reads the fact not as miraculous in itself but as leading to a display of supernatural calmness and so to the jailer's conversion, and that since the chains were fastened to rings in the wall a great shock would loosen the stones. Robertson supposes the prison excavated from rock in the hillside, so that the shock would slip the bars and shake the chains from the walls. Clarke keeps the miracle but puts the wonder elsewhere, that not one prisoner escaped though the doors were open and the bolts off. Calvin observes that the Lord could have loosed the fetters without an earthquake, but that the addition confirmed them, since he shook air and earth for their sakes, and was requisite besides so that the keeper and the rest might not think the miracle came by chance.

On the drawn sword three explain the custom and two go further. Clarke says every jailer was liable to the same penalty as his prisoner, so he chose to die by his own hand, the custom being applauded by the philosophers and sanctioned by some of their greatest men. Barnes adds the examples, that men of the first rank had fallen on their own swords, and that many did so at this very place after the great battle fought there. Ellicott presses that point hardest: suicide was a natural resource anywhere, but here there was a local predisposition, the town having been conspicuous for those who preferred death to the loss of freedom, an act looked on as heroic and naturally contagious. Robertson puts it in a word, that the Stoic philosophy had made suicide popular as the escape from trouble. Calvin alone turns the question round and asks why Paul hindered him at all, since the man's death might have opened a way of escape, so that Paul seems by preventing it to refuse the deliverance God had offered.
28:
How Paul knew what the man was about they answer alike. Gill says it was by divine revelation, since from the inner dungeon he could not have seen him unless the opened doors let in light enough, and may have known in the same way God's designs of grace toward the man's family. Clarke says that as it was midnight Paul must have had a divine intimation; Wesley agrees, calling such immediate notice by no means incredible, and explains the loud voice by earnestness and distance. Barnes makes the words the standing command of religion, forbidding men to do themselves harm not only by the sword or halter but by intemperance and dissipation; Wesley states the principle, that though the Christian faith opens the prospect into another life it absolutely forbids and effectually prevents a man's discharging himself from this. Ellicott hears in them the love that burnt in Paul's heart, for whom the suicide others would have admired would have been the most terrible of all deaths, and who could not bear that even his own gaoler should so perish in his despair.

The call for lights is read three ways. Clarke says he wanted to see whether Paul's words were true, his own safety depending on it. Gill draws the contrast, that while he was going about a work of darkness he was in no concern for a light, and called for one only when delivered from the snare. Barnes ascribes his trembling to the earthquake and to the calmness of Paul and Silas. Calvin observes what a good thing it is for men to be thrown down from their pride, since one hardened in his superstitions might have despised whatever they said, whereas fear now makes him apt to be taught.

What he meant by being saved is the disputed point. Barnes and Clarke argue alike that since not one prisoner had escaped he could not think himself in danger from Rome, and that the apostles' answer would have been no remedy for such a danger. Ellicott asks whether he was thinking of temporal safety or whether there had come upon him, in that suicidal agony, the sense of an inward misery and shame, a horror of great darkness, and thinks the latter most probable; he adds that the very circumstances which brought Paul to the prison had pointed him out as proclaiming the way of salvation, so that the witness of the possessed girl was not altogether fruitless. Robertson says it was certainly more than escape from peril, and Wesley makes it the guilt he felt and the vengeance he feared. Calvin marks that he asks counsel so as to show he will obey, where the wicked often tremble at wonders and are then made more obstinate, as Pharaoh was.

The answer given him is short, and its shortness is what they discuss. Calvin calls it a cold and hungry definition of salvation to look at, and yet perfect, since Christ alone has all the parts of blessedness included in him and is the only mark at which faith must aim, men's minds doing nothing but wander when they turn aside from him. Barnes marks what they did not say: they did not direct him to means, to prayer, or to further seeking, nor advise delay, but told him to believe at once. Gill guards it on the other side, that a bare historical faith will not serve, since there may be such a faith and no salvation, but he must look to Christ alone, rely on him and commit the care of his soul to him. Ellicott notes that the plural shows Paul was not the only teacher, and that the Greek sets the respectful title the man used against the one Lord they name; Clarke and Wesley add that the household was to receive the same, and did so and were saved.
32:
What was spoken is filled out by Ellicott: belief in Christ, unless a mere formula repeated as a charm, required explanation, so that the title itself, the acts and words that showed Jesus was the Christ, his life and death and resurrection, forgiveness and communion with him, and the outward signs appointed as witnesses, must all have been included in the word preached to that congregation so strangely assembled between midnight and dawn; even this gaoler, he says, had to be a catechumen before baptism. Barnes says they instructed the house, old and young, then baptized the whole family; Robertson calls it a remarkable service of keenest attention; Gill says they opened the word to him for his comfort.

How they were baptized is disputed three ways. Clarke argues from the word rendered straightway that there can have been no immersion, the dead of night, the general agitation and the necessity of dispatch all disproving it; and denies that washing the blood from the wounds required any pool at all. Ellicott holds that no certain answer can be given between immersion and affusion, but that a public prison was likely enough to contain a bath where the former would be feasible. Robertson canvasses the tank in which the jailer had bathed them, the basin in the court for rain, and a bath within the walls, and quotes another that the water was perhaps in the court and the baptism that of immersion, an essential part of the symbolism.

Two things about the washing are noticed. Barnes and Wesley observe that the apostles, though they had the gift of miracles, did not exercise it on their own sufferings, restoring others and not themselves; Wesley adds that it was not expedient, since it would have frustrated wise designs of God answered by their sufferings. Barnes marks the effect of religion in producing humanity, since the same man who hours before had thrust them into the inner prison with no concern for their wounds made an act of humanity one of his first once converted. Ellicott sets the two washings in suggestive juxtaposition, the jailer's of their stripes and theirs of his regeneration, he too being cleansed from worse wounds than the rods had made. Calvin marks the notable exchange, that the man lately about to murder himself because he thought his prisoners escaped now lays aside all fear and brings them home of his own accord, which shows how faith animates those who before had no heart; and that in lodging them otherwise than the magistrate had enjoined he testified that his faith was not idle. Clarke puts it as an exchange too, that as they were instruments of health to his soul he became the instrument of health to their bodies; Wesley, that faith makes a man joyful, prudent, liberal.

Why the magistrates changed their minds is the last question, and no two answer alike. Henry says the early hour intimates either that they were sensible the earthquake was meant to plead their prisoners' cause or that their consciences had smitten them, and draws the contrast that while the persecuted sang in the stocks the persecutors were full of tossings to and fro upon their beds. Barnes says an earthquake is always fitted to alarm the guilty, and was among the Romans an omen of the anger of the gods. Clarke says we cannot tell, unless we receive the reading of one manuscript adding that they came together into the court and, remembering the earthquake, were afraid; Robertson reports the same reading and allows the earthquake, Lydia's influence and a belated sense of justice together. Ellicott thinks it likelier they felt they had acted hastily in punishing without trial or inquiry, and wanted to wash their hands of the business quietly; Calvin says only that they were brought to repentance of their own accord, as commonly falls out after a sedition.
36:
Paul's refusal to slip away quietly is explained from Roman law. Barnes names three aggravating circumstances: they had been beaten contrary to law, publicly, so that the reparation ought to be as public, and without a trial while uncondemned, so that the magistrates ought themselves to come and release them and publicly acknowledge their error. Clarke names the two laws, one forbidding a citizen to be bound and the other to be beaten with rods, and quotes the orator that binding a Roman citizen is a transgression and scourging him wickedness. Ellicott recalls that this was the heaviest charge brought against a notorious governor, and that the three words by which a man claimed his citizenship acted almost like a charm in stopping provincial violence; Paul was a citizen by birth, his father probably wealthy enough to buy the privilege. Robertson calls the reply a marvel of brevity and energy, almost every word a separate indictment of the whole proceeding, Gill notes the message was brought by the jailer himself, who Ellicott says used the parting phrase in its full meaning.

Why the privilege was pleaded now and not before is answered three ways. Wesley observes that Paul does not always plead it, but that among entire strangers such treatment might have raised a suspicion of some uncommon crime and hindered the gospel. Ellicott judges his motive was less his own honour than a desire to impress the magistrates with the wrong they had done. Barnes says simply that Paul knew the privileges of a citizen and at proper times did not hesitate to assert them.

What they feared is measured differently. Barnes reports the penalty as death and confiscation, and calls their coming a most humiliating act but unavoidable, the apostles having them completely in their power. Robertson says they became frightened for their own lives, the colonists being sure to turn against them had the facts been known. Ellicott observes that their ignorance was no defence and that the tables were turned, the accused having become a possible accuser. Calvin is harder on them than any: they are not once moved by the other point, that they had handled innocent men cruelly without any inquiry, though that was the greater reproach; because they did not fear that any man would punish them they were not moved by the judgment of God, and feared only the Roman axes. Clarke adds from a manuscript a fuller apology, in which they plead ignorance that the prisoners were righteous men and beg them to leave lest an insurrection be raised again.

On the departure they are agreed. Gill says they went out publicly, with great honour, at the request of the very men who had put them there. Barnes says they besought them to depart to save their own character and prevent a further tumult, and infers from the change of person that Luke did not go with Paul and Silas; Ellicott and Robertson draw the same inference, Ellicott adding that the Evangelist seems to have made the city the centre of his work for years, and tracing to him and to Lydia the generous help afterwards sent to Paul at Thessalonica and probably at Corinth. Robertson notes that the brethren met at Lydia's house, now probably the meeting-place of the church. Calvin says they would have tarried longer had they been suffered, the magistrates' requests being imperious and armed, but did not neglect exhorting the brethren; and their going straight to Lydia is a token that though the church was increased she was still the chief of the greater number in diligence. Wesley says that though many circumstances invited their stay they wisely complied, lest they seem obstinate or vengeful or be suspected of a design to stir up the people; Clarke closes with the fruit of the visit, a church founded whose members did credit to their profession.
